summary: For ages 5–7: explore a rock pool (tide pool) as a small ocean habitat on the shore where crabs, anemones, starfish, limpets, small fish and shrimp live, and grasp ONE concrete way an animal copes with crashing waves and changing water levels. Two learning goals: (1) name at least three rock-pool residents and recognise the pool as a little sea home; (2) describe one coping adaptation (limpet clamps to rock; anemone pulls in tentacles/holds water; crab hides in a crevice). Keep the adaptation concrete and singular — deeper adaptation study belongs to a later age. Foster a 'look closely, don't disturb' observational stance. Aligns with UK KS1 Y2 living-things-and-habitats and NGSS K-ESS3-1 / 2-LS4-1 as a classic micro-habitat study.
misconceptions: 'A rock pool is just a puddle' — not seeing it as a living habitat full of animals.
'The animals are stuck there by accident' — missing that they are suited to and survive the pool's harsh, changing conditions.
'An anemone is a plant/flower' — it's an animal (the waving 'petals' are tentacles).
'Starfish are fish' — they are invertebrates (seeds the later classifying topic).
'Nothing lives in a rock pool when the tide is out' — not grasping that animals cope (clamp down, hide, hold water) until the sea returns.

activities.title: Peer into the pool and find the hidden creatures
steps: Study a detailed top-down picture of a rock pool where creatures are tucked under seaweed and in crevices, as they really are when you go rock-pooling.
Search for and point to each hidden animal (crab, anemone, starfish, limpet, small fish/blenny, shrimp) — reveal each one and learn its name.
For each creature found, uncover 'how it copes' with pool life: the limpet clamps tightly to the rock against the waves; the anemone pulls in its waving tentacles; the crab tucks under a ledge.

Change the water level from high tide (the pool covered by the sea) to low tide (the sea goes out, the rocks around the pool are uncovered, and the pool is left holding less seawater). Watch which animals clamp down, ball up, or hide away, and notice that the pool still holds seawater and is still full of life.
activities.insight: A rock pool is not just a puddle — it is a small, tough ocean home that changes as the tide comes and goes, and every animal has its own trick for surviving the waves and the sea going out.

activities.title: Help each animal survive the changing tide
steps: Watch or control a wave crashing in / the tide dropping out over the pool.
Perform each animal's coping move in time with the change: clamp the limpet flat to the rock, hide the crab under a ledge, pull in the anemone's tentacles.
Notice the consequence: if the limpet is left loose when a wave crashes, it gets swept away — if it clamps down, it stays safe.
Act out the moves with your own body too — clamp like a limpet, close up like an anemone, scuttle and hide like a crab.
activities.insight: The way an animal copes is an action with a reason: clamping, hiding and closing up are what keep these creatures safe when waves crash and the water drops — being 'adapted' means being built for these changes.

activities.title: Is the crab trapped? Talk it through
steps: Consider the claim: 'A child finds a crab and an anemone in a rock pool and says — they're trapped here, the sea left them behind, so they must be stuck and struggling. Is that right?'
Say in your own words what a rock pool is (a small ocean home, not a trap), and explain how an animal copes when waves crash and the water goes up and down.

Answer probing follow-ups: 'When a big wave crashes, what does the crab do? What does the anemone do?'; 'What makes the water go up and down during the day?'; 'Would a goldfish from a tank cope in a rock pool with salty seawater and crashing waves? Why not?'; 'If the rock pool is the animals' home, should we take them out to save them?'
activities.insight: The animals are not trapped victims — the pool is their home and they are suited to it; the discriminating idea is being able to say HOW at least one animal copes, not just feeling sorry for it.

checkQuestion: A child finds a crab and a sea anemone in a rock pool and says: 'They're trapped here — the sea left them behind, so they must be stuck and struggling.' Is that right? Tell me what a rock pool is, and how its animals actually cope when waves crash and the water level goes up and down.
checkAnswer: It's not right — the animals aren't trapped or dying; a rock pool is a small ocean habitat they are suited to live in. When waves crash and the tide changes the water level, they cope in clever ways: crabs scuttle under rocks or into cracks, anemones pull in their tentacles and close up so they don't dry out, and limpets clamp down tightly onto the rock. The pool changes with the tide, and its creatures are adapted to survive that.
